changes.local: This is another impressively large amount of energy, equivalent to about 14,000 barrels of crude oil or 600,000 gallons of gasoline. But, it is only one-fourth the energy produced by the fusion of a kilogram mixture of deuterium and tritium as seen in the previous section. Even though each fission reaction yields about ten times the energy of a fusion reaction, the energy per kilogram of fission fuel is less, because there are far fewer moles per kilogram of the heavy nuclides. Fission fuel is also much more scarce than fusion fuel, and less than 1% of uranium [MATH] is readily usable.

changes.local: Fission is the opposite of fusion and releases energy only when heavy nuclei are split. As noted in "Fusion", energy is released if the products of a nuclear reaction have a greater binding energy per nucleon ( [MATH] ) than the parent nuclei. shows that [MATH] is greater for medium-mass nuclei than heavy nuclei, implying that when a heavy nucleus is split, the products have less mass per nucleon, so that mass is destroyed and energy is released in the reaction. The amount of energy per fission reaction can be large, even by nuclear standards. The graph in shows [MATH] to be about 7.6 MeV/nucleon for the heaviest nuclei ( [MATH] about 240), while [MATH] is about 8.6 MeV/nucleon for nuclei having [MATH] about 120. Thus, if a heavy nucleus splits in half, then about 1 MeV per nucleon, or approximately 240 MeV per fission, is released. This is about 10 times the energy per fusion reaction, and about 100 times the energy of the average [MATH] , [MATH] , or [MATH] decay.
